Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
Rajesh's Reckoning

Rajesh Mehta was forty-four years old and had built a life in a way that felt, on most days, like a reasonable facsimile of safety. He worked as a sous chef at a upscale restaurant in Portland, a position he had held for seven years, and he lived alone in a modest apartment two blocks from the restaurant. He had come to America in 1996, at the age of nineteen, fleeing the escalating violence in Gujarat with his older brother Arun and their mother. They had lived in a camp in Ahmedabad for three months before the arrangements were made—three months during which Rajesh had learned to sleep with one ear toward the tent flap and to recognize the particular quality of screaming that meant the violence was moving closer.

The night that would reshape his life had come in late August of 1992. Rajesh and Arun had been helping their mother gather what remained of their family's goods from their home, which sat on the edge of a neighborhood that had begun to fracture along religious lines. The sounds had started as a distant roar—voices, chanting, the percussion of something heavy striking metal. Rajesh's mother had gripped his shoulder and pulled him toward the back room. Arun had frozen near the front window. In the next moment, a truck had plowed through the gate, and men had poured into the courtyard. Rajesh had been pushed into a storage space beneath the floorboards by his mother's hands—hands he could never quite remember the feeling of, though he carried the knowledge that they had been there. What followed existed in his mind as a series of sensations without sequence: the sound of breaking glass, his brother's voice calling his name once, the smell of kerosene, the particular silence that comes after screaming stops. When he emerged hours later, his mother was still breathing but unconscious. Arun was not there. He had been taken, or he had run—Rajesh had never known which, and that not-knowing had become its own kind of wound.

In the three decades since, Rajesh had become expert at the architecture of avoidance. He had structured his life so that certain things simply did not enter it. He would not walk through the open plaza near his apartment, even in daylight, because the exposure made his chest tighten in a way he could not articulate to anyone. When he saw a police officer or, worse, a soldier in uniform—even on television, even in a film someone was watching at the restaurant bar—his body would move toward compliance, toward making himself small and agreeable, as though his agreeableness might determine whether he lived or died. He had not watched the news in fifteen years. He changed the channel immediately if an ambulance siren appeared in a show, or if someone began describing a car accident. These were not choices, exactly; they were reflexes that had calcified into habit.

The restaurant kitchen had become his sanctuary because it was enclosed, because he could control the exits, because the noise and heat and demand for focus left no room for his mind to wander toward what he could not remember and could not forget. But three months ago, one of the prep cooks had come to work with a deep laceration on his forearm from a motorcycle accident. The wound was bandaged, but not well, and when the young man reached for a pot, the gauze had shifted. Rajesh had seen the raw edges of skin, the seeping redness, and something in him had simply stopped. He had stood motionless for several minutes, unable to move or speak. When he finally did move, he had excused himself to the walk-in cooler and remained there until his shift ended. He had not returned to the restaurant for a week. When he did, the executive chef had made it clear that reliability was not negotiable.

Now, at forty-four, Rajesh carried a guilt that had no name. He had survived when Arun had not. He had built a life, however constrained, when his mother had spent her final years in a care facility, her mind fractured by what had happened. He replayed the night constantly in a way that felt less like memory and more like a loop of accusation—he should have done something, should have been braver, should have fought instead of hidden. Sometimes when he tried to speak about it, the words would not come; the experience existed in him as sensation and silence rather than narrative. Other times he could recount the facts with a voice that sounded like it belonged to someone else, a voice completely emptied of the terror that had lived in those hours.

What had finally driven him to call a therapist was the recognition that his life was contracting. The restaurant had begun to feel unbearable. The thought of leaving his apartment was becoming harder. And the weight of having survived—of having done nothing to save the people he loved—had begun to feel like something he could not carry alone anymore.
